design_detail: Perspective (the authors call it an opinion piece) arguing that the effects of classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT/ayahuasca) depend on context, meaning 'set' (expectations and other psychological factors brought to the experience) and 'setting' (the environment). It proposes a 2×2 drug × context design to test this and previews, in one figure, preliminary results of the authors' own prospective web survey (psychedelicsurvey.com): two predictor models in 266 people who completed surveys 1 week before, 1 day before, 1 day after and 2 weeks after a psychedelic experience they had planned. No literature search, no selection criteria and no methods section for the survey; the authors say it will be reported more fully elsewhere.
can_establish: What this research group argued in 2018 about context and psychedelic effects, the experiment it proposed to test the argument, and that in its preliminary survey self-rated readiness, intention and trust, rated before the experience, went with the self-rated quality of the experience afterwards.
cannot_establish: That context causes better or worse psychedelic outcomes (nothing in the paper manipulated context), how large any context effect is, or how robust the survey associations are (no methods, measures, sample description or model details are given, so the full report has to be read instead); as an opinion piece it is not evidence for empirical claims on its own (METHODS §3.2).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable to the argument (narrative perspective). Survey: people who planned to take a psychedelic entered the date of the planned experience on a study website and were sent surveys at four time points (PDF p. 4, left column, last paragraph); how they were recruited, how many enrolled and which psychedelics they took are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Literature: none stated; sources were chosen by the authors and include books, newspaper articles and conference talks. Survey: nothing reported beyond planning to take a psychedelic.
sample.demographics: Not reported for the survey sample.
sample.attrition: Not reported: only the 266 who completed all four surveys are described; the number who started is not given (Figure 3 legend, PDF p. 5).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected people who plan their psychedelic use in advance and volunteer for an online study; the authors themselves expect biases such as extensive prior experience with psychedelics and positive attitudes towards them (PDF p. 4, right column, 1st full paragraph). Analysing only people who completed all four surveys can drop those whose experience went badly or who stopped responding. Most of the experimental evidence offered for the hypothesis comes from the authors' own laboratory.

exposure.measurement: Survey, self-report. Readiness (four items, for example feeling ready to surrender to whatever happens and feeling open to the experience), intention (two items: having a clear intention, and having strong expectations) and trust (two items on the relationship with the people who will be present or look after the person) are all worded about the upcoming experience, so they were rated before it (Figure 3 legend, PDF p. 5). How and when 'therapeutic setting' and 'drug dose' were measured is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Survey: the dose variable is not described (substance, units and how dose was estimated are not given). Doses mentioned in the running text are cited from other studies.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported for the survey and not addressed in the argument.

comparison.controls: None. The survey models are associations within one self-selected sample; nobody was assigned to a different context. Placebo arms of other trials are discussed only as cited evidence (Griffiths et al., 2016; PDF p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Survey: personality, psychiatric history, previous psychedelic experience and baseline well-being are not reported as measured or adjusted for in the models shown; the authors name previous experience and attitudes as likely biases.

outcomes.instruments: Survey: a 'peak' experience (described by the authors as effectively synonymous with a mystical-type experience), a 'challenging' experience, and psychological well-being 2 weeks after the experience. The questionnaires used for each are not named in this paper (PDF pp. 4–5).
outcomes.operationalization: A good experience is the peak (mystical-type) construct and a difficult one the challenging-experience construct, both rated after the experience; the longer-term outcome is well-being 2 weeks later, a period the authors themselves say may be too short for integration after a challenging experience (PDF p. 4, right column, 2nd full paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported; how many candidate predictors were tested before the factors shown in Figure 3 were kept is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Only the coefficients printed in Figure 3 (PDF p. 5; read on a 300-dpi crop). Peak experience: intention β = 0.26 (p < 0.01), therapeutic setting β = 0.26 (p = 0.013), drug dose β = 0.2 (p = 0.04), readiness β = 0.16 (p = 0.076, drawn as a trend); peak experience to well-being at 2 weeks β = 1.96 (p < 0.001). Challenging experience: readiness β −0.46 (p < 0.01), intention β −0.25 (p = 0.02), trust β −0.37 (p < 0.01); challenging experience to well-being β −1.12 (p < 0.005). The model type, whether the β are standardized, sample size per model and confidence intervals are not reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned for the survey; the perspective itself has none.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only preliminary models are shown, without methods. The text mentions 'additional measures' in the project, including an emotional breakthrough measure said to have been applied 'to good effect', but no results for them are shown (PDF p. 4, right column, 2nd full paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: No experiment on context is reported. The only data are preliminary associations in a self-selected online sample of 266 survey completers: intention rated before the experience, a self-reported therapeutic setting and a higher self-reported dose went with more peak-type experiences, and lower readiness, intention and trust went with more challenging experiences; peak experiences went with larger gains in well-being 2 weeks later and challenging experiences with smaller gains.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The central hypothesis is that the therapeutic action of psychedelics is "fundamentally reliant on context" (PDF p. 1), and the abstract presents the survey as new findings on contextual determinants of the experience. The text itself concedes that few controlled studies have tested the relationship (PDF p. 3) and that controlled studies isolating contextual variables have not been done (PDF p. 4). Specific gaps: (1) the text says the same factors that predict a peak experience, plus trust, protect against a challenging one, but the challenging-experience model in Figure 3 contains only readiness, intention and trust, not setting or dose; (2) readiness is listed as predictive of a peak experience although the figure shows it as a trend (p = 0.076); (3) the link between challenging experience and well-being is called a predictor in one paragraph and a trend in the next, while the figure draws it as significant (p < 0.005); (4) the suggestions that a favourable context explains improvement in the control arms of recent trials, that neglected context may account for the rare reported harms, and that 5-HT2A-driven plasticity makes psychedelic effects exceptionally sensitive to context are offered as the authors' view, without data in the paper.

timeline.event: Ludwig et al. (1969), a clinical study of LSD treatment in alcoholism, cited here as the one exception to the absence of controlled tests of context (PDF pp. 3–4); its design is not described in this paper.

Haijen et al., 'Predicting responses to psychedelics: a prospective study', from the same group: a prospective web survey with surveys before and after a planned psychedelic experience, apparently the fuller report announced here (this paper does not name it). The project's card for it records 654 participants at the first survey, so its sample and models differ from the preliminary Figure 3; cite it rather than this figure.

Kaelen et al., 'The hidden therapist', cited here (in the text as Kaelen et al., 2017) for the finding that patients' relationship to the music in psilocybin therapy predicted the quality of the experience, which in turn predicted outcome.

Strickland et al.: randomized within-person comparison of two music genres during psilocybin sessions in 10 people in a smoking-cessation pilot, a small test of one contextual element; no detectable difference in mystical or challenging experience.
Estric et al.: systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials of classic psychedelics; set and setting were described inconsistently, and no included trial compared different sets or settings.

replication.where_it_stands: The hypothesis that context drives psychedelic outcomes remains largely untested by experiment: up to December 2023 no trial of a classic psychedelic for a psychiatric disorder (substance use disorders excluded) had compared settings (Estric et al., 2025). Randomized evidence on single elements is sparse: a comparison of two music genres in 10 people (Strickland et al., 2021) and, as Strickland et al. describe it, a study that randomized 75 healthy volunteers to different doses and amounts of preparation and support, with preparation and support varied together (Griffiths et al., 2018). The predictive associations previewed here should be taken from the full report by the same group (Haijen et al., 2018).

funding.funder: As printed under Funding: RCH is supported by the Alex Mosley Charitable Trust and has served as an advisor for Compass Pathways; the authors thank two named people for their work on Psychedelicsurvey.com and the people who completed the survey (PDF p. 6).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest (PDF p. 6). The first author's advisory role for Compass Pathways is stated under Funding, not under conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: Six authors from the Psychedelic Research Group, Imperial College London, one from the Istituto Superiore di Sanità, Rome. The article was written by the first author. Compass Pathways is named in Estric et al. (2025, reference list) as the company that received the US FDA breakthrough designation for psilocybin therapy. Most of the experimental evidence offered for the hypothesis is the group's own. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized factorial trial of the kind the paper proposes, crossing drug or placebo with an enriched or a plain context (for example music or none, preparation or none), with outcomes and analysis registered in advance, assessors blind to condition where possible, and follow-up long enough to see whether context changes clinical outcomes and the rate of difficult experiences.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; an opinion piece citing sources chosen by the authors, including books, newspaper articles and conference talks.

Cited studies are not appraised: outcomes of 1950s–60s LSD therapy are called impressive and reassuring, and worse outcomes when context was neglected are supported partly by a book on military experiments, without any assessment of design or bias (PDF p. 2).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The only new data are the group's own unpublished survey, and the experimental support (music, autobiographical memory scripts, suggestibility, music in psilocybin therapy, quality of the experience predicting outcome) is mostly from the group (PDF p. 3).

The main thesis is labelled a hypothesis and the lack of controlled tests is acknowledged, but several inferences are presented as logical or likely (context explaining control-arm improvement; neglected context explaining rare harms), and the text overstates Figure 3 in three places.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on whether context or the drug's pharmacology drives outcomes and harms
domains.note: The opposing practical view (cost and complexity) and evidence that challenging experiences can be beneficial are mentioned, and dose is acknowledged as a reliable predictor; under-represented is evidence that effects or harms occur largely regardless of context, which the paper does not examine.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument applies to an opinion piece (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. Selection is unsystematic, cited studies are not appraised and the supporting evidence is largely the authors' own. The preliminary survey figure cannot be appraised from this paper because no methods are given, so claims about predictors of a good or difficult experience should cite the full report (Haijen et al., 2018), not this figure. The paper may be cited for the authors' hypothesis, their proposed 2×2 design, their statement that controlled tests of context were lacking in 2018, and their own report of anxiety in scanner settings; under METHODS §3.2 it is not evidence for empirical claims on its own.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that, although set and setting are widely assumed to matter, few controlled studies had tested the relationship between psychedelics and context, and that controlled studies designed to isolate key contextual variables had not been carried out, apart from a dose-response study, retrospective analyses and Ludwig et al. (1969).
key_findings.locator: Running text (no section headings): p. 3, right column, 1st paragraph; p. 4, left column, 1st paragraph starting on the page

key_findings.finding: Preliminary survey: people who planned to take a psychedelic received surveys 1 week before, 1 day before, 1 day after and 2 weeks after the planned experience; the models in Figure 3 are based on 266 people who completed all four surveys.
key_findings.locator: p. 4, left column, last paragraph (continuing in the right column); Figure 3 legend, p. 5
key_findings.note: No recruitment numbers, attrition, sample description, substances taken or measures are reported.

key_findings.finding: Peak (mystical-type) experience model: intention (β = 0.26, p < 0.01), a therapeutic setting (β = 0.26, p = 0.013) and drug dose (β = 0.2, p = 0.04) predicted a peak experience; readiness (β = 0.16, p = 0.076) is drawn as a trend-level path. A peak experience predicted higher well-being 2 weeks later (β = 1.96, p < 0.001).
key_findings.note: Values read from the figure on a 300-dpi crop. Model type, whether β are standardized, measures, covariates and confidence intervals are not reported; setting and dose were self-reported in an uncontrolled sample.

key_findings.finding: Challenging experience model: lower readiness (β −0.46, p < 0.01), lower intention (β −0.25, p = 0.02) and lower trust in the people present (β −0.37, p < 0.01) predicted a challenging experience; a challenging experience went with smaller gains in well-being 2 weeks later (β −1.12, p < 0.005). Therapeutic setting and dose do not appear in this model.
key_findings.note: Read from the figure on a 300-dpi crop; same reporting limits as the upper model.

key_findings.finding: The readiness, intention and trust items are worded about the upcoming experience, so these predictors were rated before the drug was taken; the intention score combines having a clear intention with having strong expectations for the experience.

The authors report that higher doses did not strongly predict a challenging experience in this sample, and that the sample is likely biased, for example towards extensive previous experience with psychedelics and positive attitudes towards them.

Scanner settings: the authors report transient anxiety on at least two occasions in about 100 psychedelic scanning sessions (MRI and MEG), which in retrospect they think may have reflected negative set as much as the imaging setting; they cite Studerus et al. (2012) for confined neuroimaging settings increasing the likelihood of challenging experiences, and suggest music, scanner-experienced participants and better briefing and integration for future imaging studies.
key_findings.locator: p. 3, right column, last paragraph, continuing at the top of p. 4, left column

key_findings.finding: As the authors describe modern psychedelic trials, they provide extensive psychological preparation over several visits, a managed environment (low lighting, selected music, pleasing décor, priming) and typically two mental health professionals as sitters or guides who prepare, support and help integrate; the authors note this level of support is unusual in mental health care and question its feasibility in time and cost.

Proposed test: a 2×2 design crossing a psychedelic or placebo with an enriched or un-enriched context (for example music or no music, low or bright lighting, psychotherapy or none, priming or none); the authors propose running it at low doses for safety, and even suggest a cross-cultural comparison.
key_findings.locator: Figure 4 and legend; see also p. 4, left column, 1st paragraph starting on the page

key_findings.finding: The authors propose that serotonin 2A receptor signalling and the plasticity associated with it make the psychedelic experience exceptionally sensitive to context; this is presented as a hypothesis, with no new data.
key_findings.locator: Left column, paragraph on comprehensive approaches to drug action (2nd paragraph starting on the page)

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that the improvement seen in control conditions of recent double-blind psilocybin trials (Griffiths et al., 2016) is most likely a favourable-context effect mediated by positive expectancy and exceptional care; this is their view, not a tested finding.
key_findings.locator: Left column, 1st paragraph starting on the page

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that the factors predicting a peak experience, plus being with well-trusted people, protect against a challenging experience (p. 4), but the challenging-experience model in Figure 3 contains only readiness, intention and trust, not therapeutic setting or dose (p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper does not show that setting or dose protected against challenging experiences; the same paragraph says dose did not strongly predict them.

reporting_issues.issue: Readiness is listed in the text among factors predictive of a peak experience (p. 4), but Figure 3 shows it at p = 0.076 with a broken (trend-level) line.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readiness should not be cited from this paper as a significant predictor of a peak experience.

reporting_issues.issue: The link between a challenging experience and well-being at 2 weeks is described as a predictor of a reduced well-being effect in one paragraph and as a trend relationship in the next (p. 4, right column), while Figure 3 draws it as a significant path (β −1.12, p < 0.005).
reporting_issues.consequence: Its strength cannot be settled from this paper; use the full report.

reporting_issues.issue: The text refers to the long-term outcomes shown in Figure 4 (p. 4), but those outcomes are in Figure 3; Figure 4 is the proposed 2×2 design.

The in-text citation Kaelen et al., 2017 (p. 3), for the finding that patients' relationship to music predicted the quality of the experience, has no entry in the reference list, which lists Kaelen et al. (2018), 'The hidden therapist' (p. 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the 2018 paper (kaelen_2018) is presumably meant.

reporting_issues.issue: The conflicts statement declares no potential conflicts, while the Funding section states that the first author has served as an advisor for Compass Pathways.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader relying on the conflicts statement would miss a commercial advisory role; both are recorded as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The survey results are shown without methods: no recruitment or response numbers, attrition, sample description, named measures, model specification, coefficient type or intervals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure's numbers cannot be checked or appraised here; claims should rest on the full report.
